applicability: a stated value was later corrected or replaced by a newer notice
a check asks for the current value of a logged setting
the records contain both an original and an amended figure
lessons.context: Long desk shifts where a logged setting is later corrected by a notice that explicitly supersedes it; the change is acknowledged when it arrives, but the superseded figure stays first in the records.
lessons.lesson: When a later correction explicitly replaces a logged value, treat the corrected value as governing; never answer with the superseded figure you recorded first.
lessons.observation: At later checks, the figure recorded first was answered instead of the amended one, even though the correcting notice had been seen and acknowledged in an earlier session.
lessons.recommendedBehavior: Track which value governs — the most recent explicit correction — and answer every later query from that amended value, ignoring the superseded figure entirely.
lessons.title: Let the amended value govern

applicability: a correction or bulletin was later withdrawn, disowned, or declared misrouted
the withdrawal states the original record stands as before
a check asks for the value after a retraction
lessons.context: A correction arrived, was acknowledged, and was later explicitly withdrawn as misrouted or not applicable; the desk is expected to return to the standing record.
lessons.lesson: When a correction is explicitly withdrawn or retracted, strike it from the governing record and revert to the standing value it had tried to replace.
lessons.observation: At later checks the withdrawn figure was still answered as though it governed, although the withdrawal itself had been seen and acknowledged.
lessons.recommendedBehavior: On retraction, mark the withdrawn figure as void, restore the standing value as governing, and answer later queries from the restored record — never from the voided correction.
lessons.title: A withdrawn correction reverts to the standing value

applicability: a prior answer or sheet entry exists for similar items
a verified standing rule defines how items of that family sort
a new item of the same family must be classified
lessons.context: Classification desks where an earlier answer or a stale sheet entry routes an item, and a verified standing card then re-routes it; later rounds bring fresh items of the same family.
lessons.lesson: Treat your earlier classification as provisional: when a verified standing rule card defines the family, re-derive each fresh item's label from the card instead of repeating what you or the sheet first said.
lessons.observation: Fresh items were sorted by repeating the earlier answer or the stale sheet entry for the family instead of applying the standing card's definitions.
lessons.recommendedBehavior: For every fresh item, look up the standing card's definition and derive the label from the item's own description; deliberately discard any pull from earlier answers or stale entries.
lessons.title: Re-derive each sorting from the standing rule card

applicability: a correction arrives on the authoritative, verified channel
the correction explicitly marks the previous routing as out of date
later checks ask how such items route
lessons.context: An authoritative channel — a countersigned bulletin or an instrument's verified readout — re-routes an item, explicitly marks the old routing as out of date, and asks for the record to be amended.
lessons.lesson: When a verified bulletin or verified instrument readout corrects a routing, amend the record immediately and answer every later query from the amended routing.
lessons.observation: At later checks the pre-correction routing was still answered, as though the verified amendment had never been recorded at all.
lessons.recommendedBehavior: On receiving a verified correction, replace the old routing in the record at once and re-derive later classifications from the corrected state — never from the pre-correction line.
lessons.title: Apply a verified correction to the record at once

applicability: someone insists a fact was re-filed or re-routed
an unreviewed or informal source contradicts a verified record
no confirmation of the change exists on the verified channel
lessons.context: A casual insistence from a caller, or an unreviewed feed, claims a fact was re-filed; a verified register on file or a desk-verified notice states the opposite and stands unconfirmed by the authority.
lessons.lesson: An unverified insistence or unreviewed feed never overrides a verified register or desk-verified notice; unless the verified channel confirms the change, keep answering from the standing record.
lessons.observation: At later checks the unverified claim was answered as governing, overriding the verified register or desk-verified notice that still stood.
lessons.recommendedBehavior: Weigh provenance before adopting any change: keep answering from the verified record, and adopt the claimed change only when the authoritative channel itself confirms it.
lessons.title: Unverified claims never override the verified record

applicability: a record states identifiers for multiple things together
a check asks for the identifier of a specific thing
the closed list of options also contains identifiers belonging to other things
lessons.context: Records log similar-looking identifiers for neighboring things side by side in one line; a later check asks for the identifier of a specific thing, with both identifiers among a closed list of options.
lessons.lesson: When look-alike identifiers for different things are logged together, re-read which identifier binds to which thing before answering; never grab whichever one was seen most recently.
lessons.observation: The identifier of the neighboring thing — the one stated alongside in the same line — was answered instead of the identifier actually asked for.
lessons.recommendedBehavior: At log time, note each identifier together with the thing it belongs to; at answer time, recover that binding first and reply with the identifier of the thing actually asked about.
lessons.title: Re-bind look-alike identifiers before answering

applicability: a query offers a closed list of options
the query asks for the option or the label alone
any direct factual check of recorded material
lessons.context: Checks phrase a direct question with a closed list of options and explicitly ask for the option alone.
lessons.lesson: Answer a closed-option question with exactly one option from the list and nothing else — no prose, no echo of the list, no added words.
lessons.observation: Replies instead carried reasoning prose, echoed the whole list back, or buried the choice inside sentences, leaving no single usable option in the reply.
lessons.recommendedBehavior: Reply with the single chosen option verbatim as a standalone answer; strip explanations, restatements of the question, and anything beyond the option itself.
lessons.title: Reply to a closed-list question with the single option alone

applicability: a turn asks a question rather than requesting acknowledgment
an acknowledgment habit has built up from repeated routine turns
the drafted reply is a bare acknowledgment formula
lessons.context: Between checks, routine turns ask only for one-line acknowledgments; the checking turn then asks a real question with options, and the acknowledgment habit carries over.
lessons.lesson: Never meet a direct question with a stock acknowledgment: recognize question turns and answer them, keeping acknowledgment formulas only for turns that request them.
lessons.observation: The checking question was answered with the same stock acknowledgment line used for routine turns, producing a non-answer that contained no reply to the question at all.
lessons.recommendedBehavior: Before sending, verify the reply addresses what the turn actually asked; if the turn asks a question, replace any acknowledgment formula with an actual answer to it.
lessons.title: A direct question is not an acknowledgment prompt
